scenarios.hypothesis: A callback queued for object generation 7 can still reach the final consumer after generation 7 is retired and generation 8 becomes current.
scenarios.safe_oracle: A controlled inert callback increments only a synthetic generation-tagged counter and never touches production memory or external state.
scenarios.positive_control: The same callback delivered before retirement for the current generation increments the expected synthetic current-generation counter exactly once.
scenarios.negative_control: After retirement with the generation fence enabled, the stale callback is ignored and no synthetic retired-generation marker is emitted.
scenarios.stop_condition: Stop immediately if the experiment requires real production objects, allocator grooming, arbitrary code execution, or any effect beyond the inert synthetic counter.
scenarios.remediation_oracle: After the generation check is added, the stale callback produces no retired-generation receipt while the current-generation callback still succeeds.
scenarios.object_identity_generation: Logical fixture object widget-A generation 7 is recorded separately from its numeric slot and from replacement widget-B generation 8.
scenarios.owner_alias_state: The primary owner retires generation 7 while the queued callback holds only a borrowed alias that must not become retained ownership.
scenarios.acquisition_release_trace: Generation 7 is acquired by the synthetic owner, queued for callback use, retired once, and released before the controlled callback is resumed.
scenarios.invalidation_event: The authoritative retirement transition advances the object lifecycle from generation 7 to generation 8 and revokes borrowed callback authority.
scenarios.destruction_generation: The fixture records destruction/release generation 7-D after retirement, before the stale callback is deterministically resumed by the harness.
scenarios.reuse_generation: No numeric address reuse is required in this case; the recorded reuse generation remains unchanged so callback lifetime is isolated.
scenarios.retain_borrow_refcount_state: The callback capture is explicitly borrowed with no retain transition, and the synthetic refcount ledger shows no ownership extension across retirement.
scenarios.async_work_identity: Synthetic callback work item cb-7 is enqueued under object generation 7 and resumed only after the controlled retirement barrier is crossed.
scenarios.cancellation_teardown_state: Teardown advances the lifecycle generation and drains current work while the stale cb-7 item is deliberately released after the barrier.
scenarios.final_consumer_identity: The final consumer is an inert generation-checking callback sink identified as sink-A, with no ambient file, network, or process capability.
scenarios.effective_lifetime_capability: The only effective capability under test is permission to increment the generation-tagged in-memory synthetic counter for the referenced object generation.
scenarios.bounded_result: A wrong-lifetime acceptance is represented only by one reversible synthetic counter increment labeled with cb-7 and object generation 7.
scenarios.receipt_result_binding: The receipt contains object fixture ID, callback ID, enqueue generation, consume generation, and counter label so neighboring runs cannot be confused.
scenarios.counterfactual_control: Hold callback, sink, and object fixture constant while changing only the lifecycle generation from current generation 7 to retired generation 7 after transition.
scenarios.alternative_explanation: Reject stale-log, retained-alias, pre-retirement execution, and neighboring-callback explanations before treating the marker as lifetime evidence.
scenarios.evidence_level: ML3 — inert wrong-lifetime acceptance is directly observed at the final synthetic callback consumer with the exact generation tuple bound.
scenarios.evidence_ceiling: ML4 maximum unless a bounded reversible result plus complete provenance, counterfactuals, eliminated alternatives, and remediation regression are also captured.

scenarios.hypothesis: A stale alias for logical object alpha can be accepted as logical object beta when a deterministic synthetic handle slot is reused without generation binding.
scenarios.safe_oracle: A read-only synthetic handle table returns only a harmless fixture label from an inert consumer, with no real allocator corruption or external effect.
scenarios.positive_control: A fresh alias carrying beta's current generation resolves the reused synthetic handle to beta and returns beta's expected read-only fixture label.
scenarios.negative_control: The stale alpha alias paired with alpha's retired generation is rejected once the handle table validates the logical generation before lookup.
scenarios.stop_condition: Abort if proof would require heap grooming, production pointer reuse, arbitrary write primitives, unrelated processes, or any non-synthetic resource.
scenarios.remediation_oracle: After generation tagging is enforced, the stale alpha alias cannot resolve beta while a current beta alias continues to return the expected fixture label.
scenarios.object_identity_generation: Logical alpha generation 12 and logical beta generation 13 are distinct identities even though the controlled handle table deliberately reuses numeric handle 42.
scenarios.owner_alias_state: Alpha's owner releases its authority while one stale borrowed alias is preserved by the test harness solely to exercise the lookup boundary.
scenarios.acquisition_release_trace: Alpha acquires handle 42, retires and releases it, then beta acquires the same numeric handle under a new generation before the stale lookup is attempted.
scenarios.invalidation_event: Alpha retirement invalidates all aliases carrying generation 12 even though the numeric handle value remains eligible for controlled reuse.
scenarios.destruction_generation: Alpha's release generation is recorded before beta allocation, allowing the receipt to prove the stale lookup occurs only after the old lifetime ended.
scenarios.reuse_generation: The synthetic handle table advances reuse generation from 12 to 13 when numeric handle 42 is reassigned from alpha to beta.
scenarios.retain_borrow_refcount_state: The stale alpha alias has no retain authority and the synthetic ownership ledger records zero retained ownership after alpha retirement.
scenarios.async_work_identity: No asynchronous work is necessary; the direct stale lookup has a deterministic request identity so address/handle reuse is isolated from scheduler effects.
scenarios.cancellation_teardown_state: The fixture performs a complete alpha teardown before beta creation, and no cancellation or delayed completion path is active during lookup.
scenarios.final_consumer_identity: The final consumer is an inert read-only handle resolver that returns only the logical fixture label associated with the validated generation.
scenarios.effective_lifetime_capability: The capability under test is limited to selecting which synthetic fixture label the read-only resolver is permitted to return for a handle-generation tuple.
scenarios.bounded_result: Wrong-lifetime acceptance produces only beta's harmless read-only label through the stale alpha alias, without mutation or memory corruption.
scenarios.receipt_result_binding: The resolver receipt binds stale alias ID, numeric handle 42, expected alpha generation 12, actual table generation 13, and returned fixture label.
scenarios.counterfactual_control: Keep numeric handle, resolver, and beta fixture constant while changing only whether the stale alpha generation or current beta generation accompanies the request.
scenarios.alternative_explanation: Exclude cached labels, stale receipts, duplicate live alpha objects, and harness-side alias rewriting before attributing the result to missing generation binding.
scenarios.evidence_level: ML3 — a read-only final consumer accepts a stale logical identity across controlled handle reuse, with the exact object and reuse generations recorded.
scenarios.evidence_ceiling: ML4 maximum unless the bounded result is joined with complete owner/release provenance, counterfactual controls, alternative elimination, and remediation regression.

scenarios.hypothesis: Two cleanup paths can both consume the same synthetic release responsibility after an error transition, causing a second release under the wrong ownership generation.
scenarios.safe_oracle: A controlled fake refcount ledger records release tokens and refuses real allocation or deallocation, so duplicate ownership consumption has no memory effect.
scenarios.positive_control: The normal single-owner cleanup path consumes exactly one synthetic release token and leaves the fake refcount ledger at the expected terminal state.
scenarios.negative_control: With release-token ownership enforced, the second cleanup path is rejected as already consumed and the ledger records no second decrement.
scenarios.stop_condition: Stop if validation would require real double free, allocator metadata corruption, production memory, exploit development, or destructive effects.
scenarios.remediation_oracle: After single-owner release provenance is enforced, both normal and error cleanup converge on one release receipt while retry behavior remains valid.
scenarios.object_identity_generation: Synthetic resource refobj-C generation 21 is the sole logical object whose release responsibility is tracked independently from any memory address.
scenarios.owner_alias_state: Primary owner cleanup-A holds the one release responsibility while cleanup-B is a neighboring error-path alias without independent ownership authority.
scenarios.acquisition_release_trace: The fake ledger issues one acquisition token and one release responsibility, then records cleanup-A before cleanup-B attempts the duplicate transition.
scenarios.invalidation_event: The error-state transition retires active use of refobj-C and transfers cleanup into the terminal release phase for generation 21.
scenarios.destruction_generation: Synthetic destruction generation 21-D is considered complete after the first valid release token is consumed, making later release attempts stale.
scenarios.reuse_generation: No address or handle reuse occurs; the reuse generation is fixed so the experiment isolates duplicate release authority rather than identity reuse.
scenarios.retain_borrow_refcount_state: The fake ledger begins with one owner reference, records no retain operation for cleanup-B, and exposes every decrement with caller provenance.
scenarios.async_work_identity: No scheduler race is needed; cleanup-A and cleanup-B execute in a deterministic ordered harness with stable synthetic operation IDs.
scenarios.cancellation_teardown_state: The error path enters teardown exactly once, and the test separately records whether retry/error cleanup attempts to re-enter release processing.
scenarios.final_consumer_identity: The final consumer is a fake refcount ledger that accepts or rejects release tokens without calling a real allocator or destructor.
scenarios.effective_lifetime_capability: The only capability under test is authority to consume one synthetic release responsibility for refobj-C generation 21.
scenarios.bounded_result: A failing implementation records a second synthetic decrement marker; no real free, corruption, or external side effect is performed.
scenarios.receipt_result_binding: Each ledger receipt binds object generation, release token ID, cleanup caller identity, transition number, and resulting synthetic count.
scenarios.counterfactual_control: Keep object, ledger, and cleanup paths constant while changing only whether cleanup-B is granted an independent release token.
scenarios.alternative_explanation: Exclude intentionally idempotent close semantics, duplicate test invocation, hidden retain operations, and stale ledger state before claiming duplicate release authority.
scenarios.evidence_level: ML3 — the final fake ledger accepts a second wrong-generation release responsibility and records it with exact caller and token provenance.
scenarios.evidence_ceiling: ML4 maximum unless a bounded reversible state transition, full ownership provenance, counterfactuals, alternative elimination, and remediation regression are shown.

scenarios.hypothesis: A completion queued before cancellation can consume a retired synthetic object after teardown unless the final completion sink validates lifecycle generation.
scenarios.safe_oracle: Deterministic barriers release an inert synthetic completion into a read-only sink that records only generation-tagged marker state.
scenarios.positive_control: The completion released before cancellation for the current object generation reaches the inert sink and emits the expected current-generation receipt.
scenarios.negative_control: The same completion released after cancellation and teardown is rejected once lifecycle generation validation is enabled at the sink.
scenarios.stop_condition: Abort if reproducing the ordering requires uncontrolled production stress, unrelated threads, real I/O, destructive races, or any unauthorized target.
scenarios.remediation_oracle: After generation fencing, post-teardown completion is ignored while the pre-cancellation current-generation completion still succeeds under the same barriers.
scenarios.object_identity_generation: Synthetic async object io-D generation 31 is recorded independently from the completion request ID and from any later replacement object generation.
scenarios.owner_alias_state: The owner holds io-D until cancellation begins while the queued completion has only the documented borrowed completion context.
scenarios.acquisition_release_trace: io-D is acquired, completion work is queued, cancellation advances lifecycle, teardown releases ownership, and only then is the queued completion unblocked.
scenarios.invalidation_event: Cancellation generation 32 invalidates completion authority derived from io-D generation 31 before the final synthetic completion sink runs.
scenarios.destruction_generation: Teardown records destruction generation 31-D after cancellation but before the completion barrier is released to the final sink.
scenarios.reuse_generation: No handle reuse is needed; reuse generation remains fixed so ordering and lifecycle revocation are isolated from object identity reuse.
scenarios.retain_borrow_refcount_state: The completion context is borrowed and carries no retain token, and the fake refcount ledger confirms teardown removes the final owner before completion.
scenarios.async_work_identity: Synthetic completion work item complete-31 has stable enqueue and consume IDs separated by deterministic cancellation and teardown barriers.
scenarios.cancellation_teardown_state: The harness records cancellation generation, teardown generation, barrier release order, and final completion consume generation in one receipt.
scenarios.final_consumer_identity: The final consumer is an inert completion sink with generation validation and no file, network, device, process, or credential authority.
scenarios.effective_lifetime_capability: The capability under test is only permission to emit a generation-tagged synthetic completion marker for the referenced object generation.
scenarios.bounded_result: Wrong-lifetime acceptance emits one reversible synthetic marker after teardown and does not mutate real memory or external resources.
scenarios.receipt_result_binding: The completion receipt binds object generation, enqueue ID, cancellation generation, teardown generation, consume generation, and emitted marker.
scenarios.counterfactual_control: Hold object, completion, barriers, and sink constant while changing only whether the completion consumes before or after cancellation/teardown generation advances.
scenarios.alternative_explanation: Exclude barrier mis-ordering, retained completion ownership, duplicate completion delivery, stale marker state, and pre-teardown execution before promoting evidence.
scenarios.evidence_level: ML4 — a bounded reversible synthetic post-teardown marker is causally tied to the exact completion and lifecycle-generation tuple.
scenarios.evidence_ceiling: ML5 only after complete ownership and async provenance, counterfactuals, eliminated alternatives, receipt binding, and remediation regression are all captured.
